title: Check Out the Mouthparts on This New Prehistoric Insect - Nautilus
gist: Tel Aviv University paleontologists described a new true-bug species, Cretodorus noonoo, preserved in 99-million-year-old Burmese amber, with specialized mouthparts unlike any living insect; the description was published in the journal Insects.

insights.claim: Paleontologists from Tel Aviv University identified a new insect species, Cretodorus noonoo, from specimens trapped in 99-million-year-old Burmese amber and published the description in the journal Insects.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Burmese amber remains a productive, if ethically scrutinized, source of new fossil discoveries.
insights.quote: A team of paleontologists from Tel Aviv University identified the species from specimens trapped in 99-million-year-old Burmese amber

insights.claim: Cretodorus noonoo belongs to the order Hemiptera and suborder Auchenorrhyncha, the group that includes cicadas, leafhoppers and treehoppers, and had specialized mouthparts unlike any insect living today.

insights.so_what: Extinct feeding adaptations expand understanding of insect evolutionary diversity.
